pageTitle: Cellular Reprogramming and Immortality: Expression Profiling Reveals Putative Genes Involved in Turritopsis dohrnii's Life Cycle Reversal
quote: medusae of T. dohrnii that are stressed, damaged, or senescent settle on a surface and transform into a cyst stage that, in 24–72 h, metamorphoses back into a single juvenile polyp (...). By asexual reproduction, the polyp can develop into a larger colony (i.e., colonial polyp) that can then release new medusae.
unsupported: "collapses its bell into a small blob" (the paper says the medusa settles and transforms into a cyst, with no description of the bell)
correctedFact: The reset is not instant. A stressed, damaged or aging Turritopsis dohrnii settles onto a surface and transforms into a cyst, and within 24 to 72 hours that cyst turns back into a single juvenile polyp. The polyp can then grow into a colony that releases brand new jellyfish.
note: The Natural History Museum (London) page used for 202 describes a "blob-like cyst" but gives 24 to 36 hours for the new polyp, so the 24 to 72 hour range rests on this paper.

pageTitle: Immortal jellyfish: The secret to cheating death
quote: This phenomenon has been likened to that of a butterfly which, instead of dying, would be able to transform back into a caterpillar and then metamorphose into an adult butterfly once again. The process behind this small jellyfish’s remarkable transformation is called transdifferentiation. It’s extremely rare. ... Transdifferentiation reprogrammes the medusa’s specialised cells to become specialised polyp cells
unsupported: "such as muscle becoming nerve"; "One researcher described" (the page says the process "has been likened" to a butterfly turning back into a caterpillar and names no researcher)
correctedFact: The immortal jellyfish rebuilds itself through transdifferentiation, an extremely rare process that reprograms the adult jellyfish's specialized cells into the specialized cells of a polyp. The whole reversal has been likened to a butterfly that, instead of dying, turns back into a caterpillar and later becomes a butterfly again.
note: Search results credit the butterfly comparison to Ferdinando Boero and to Shin Kubota, but The Biologist (Royal Society of Biology) feature returned 404 and the AMNH page blocked access, so no named-researcher page was read.

pageTitle: Immortal jellyfish: The secret to cheating death
quote: The hydrozoan Turritopsis dohrnii , an animal about 4.5 millimetres wide and tall – likely making it smaller than the nail on your little finger – can actually reverse its life cycle. ... It’s tiny and translucent ... researchers found that immortal jellyfish in tropical regions like Panama had only eight tentacles, whereas those in more temperate waters, such as in the Mediterranean and Japan, can have 24 or more.
unsupported: "with a bright red stomach glowing through a nearly transparent bell"; "ringed by dozens of white tentacles" (the page gives eight tentacles in Panama and 24 or more in the Mediterranean and Japan, with no color)
correctedFact: For all its fame, Turritopsis dohrnii is easy to miss. A grown adult is only about 4.5 mm wide and tall, likely smaller than the nail on your little finger. It is tiny and translucent, and even its tentacle count varies: eight in tropical Panama, 24 or more in the Mediterranean and Japan.
note: Search snippets attribute the red stomach and white tentacles to AMNH pages, but amnh.org returned a CAPTCHA and 403, so they could not be read.

pageTitle: A silent invasion
quote: Medusae of Turritopsis, however, when starved or damaged, are able to revert their life cycle ... They can thus easily survive through long journeys in cargo ships and ballast waters. We have identified a clade of the mitochondrial 16S gene in Turritopsis which contains individuals collected from Japan, the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of Panama, Florida, Spain, and Italy differing from each other in only an average of 0.31% of their base-pairs. Fifteen individuals from Japan, Atlantic Panama, Spain, and Italy shared the same haplotype. ... contributes to making this grand scale invasion a silent one.
unsupported: "came back identical" (the sequences differed by an average of 0.31%, and only 15 animals from four of the countries shared one haplotype); "spread across the planet recently" (not stated); "One scientist called it" (the paper has two authors, Miglietta and Lessios, and uses the phrase as its title)
correctedFact: When researchers compared immortal jellyfish from Japan, both coasts of Panama, Florida, Spain and Italy, a mitochondrial gene differed by only 0.31% on average, and 15 animals from four countries shared the same sequence. The authors see a human-mediated worldwide invasion carried by cargo ships and ballast water, and titled their paper "A silent invasion."
note: Abstract read through Europe PMC; the Springer and Smithsonian repository pages blocked access. Published online 2008 (volume dated 2009).

pageTitle: Female dolphins use individual vocal labels to track coercive males
quote: we investigated how females assess males by conducting 34 sound playbacks to 17 females and using drone-mounted video to analyze their behavioral responses to individual male identity signals. ... Females who were reproductively available showed a significantly stronger aversive response to the identity signals of males who coerced females at higher rates, suggesting that females track male behavior across time and use individual vocal labels to guide reproductive decision-making based on their experience of individual male behavior.
unsupported: "11 adult males" and "Shark Bay" (not in the abstract); "going on each male's track record across the population, not just their own encounters with him" (the abstract says females respond "based on their experience of individual male behavior")
correctedFact: In a 2026 study, researchers ran 34 sound playbacks of individual male dolphins' identity calls to 17 wild females and filmed the responses by drone. Females who could conceive showed a much stronger aversive response to the calls of males who coerced females at higher rates, suggesting they track each male's behavior over time.
note: News coverage (National Geographic, Smithsonian) places the study in Shark Bay, Western Australia. The PNAS full text sat behind a bot check and the PMC copy is embargoed until December 2026, so only the abstract was read.

pageTitle: Identification and Characteristics of Signature Whistles in Wild Bottlenose Dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) from Namibia
quote: The signature whistle is learned within the first year of life [15] ... Once formed, the frequency modulation pattern remains stable over decades [9], [19] ... Since signature whistles make up around 50% of the whistle repertoire in freely interacting animals [22]
unsupported: "so identity is most of the conversation" (the source says around 50%, which is half, not most)
correctedFact: A dolphin's signature whistle is not something it is born with. Calves learn theirs within the first year of life, and once the pattern forms it stays stable for decades. Signature whistles also make up around half of the whistles that freely interacting dolphins produce, so identity is a big share of the conversation.
extraPoints: Signature whistles make up about half of all whistles in freely interacting dolphins

publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (2013)
pageTitle: Vocal copying of individually distinctive signature whistles in bottlenose dolphins
quote: Copying occurred almost exclusively between close associates such as mother–calf pairs and male alliances during separation and was not followed by aggression. All copies were clearly recognizable as such because copiers consistently modified some acoustic parameters of a signal when copying it. ... Signature whistle copying is, however, rare ... on average 4.4 parameters (range: 1–6) differed significantly between the copy and the original signature whistle.

pageTitle: Bottlenose dolphins can use learned vocal labels to address each other
quote: We investigated this in experiments on wild, free-ranging bottlenose dolphins off the east coast of Scotland. ... Although both the copy treatment and unfamiliar control whistles were predominantly synthetic to remove voice features ... Animals responded to hearing their signature whistle by calling back for 8 of the 12 copy playback treatments. ... Animals did not respond to whistles that were not their own signature.
unsupported: "stripping out every trace of the original animal's voice" (the copy stimuli were "predominantly synthetic", not all); "none responded to whistles that were not theirs" (the abstract says so, but the results report matching calls after two familiar-control playbacks, and none after unfamiliar ones)
correctedFact: Off the coast of Scotland, researchers played wild dolphins synthetic copies of their own signature whistles, built to remove the voice features of the original caller. Dolphins called back with their own whistle in 8 of 12 of these playbacks, and responded far less to whistles that were not theirs. The identity is in the shape of the sound.

pageTitle: Precocious development of self-awareness in dolphins
quote: Two captive born young bottlenose dolphins, Bayley (female, age 3.5 months) and Foster (male, age 14 months), were exposed to a one-way mirror with their social group ... housed at the National Aquarium in Baltimore, MD. ... On Bayley’s 4 th day of mirror exposure (age 5.5 months), we first observed instances of self-directed behavior. ... both dolphins exhibited MSR, indicated by self-directed behavior at the mirror, at ages earlier than generally reported for children and at ages much earlier than reported for chimpanzees. ... MSR, as evidenced by self-directed behavior, first emerges between 12–15 months
unsupported: "What mirror behavior proves about self-awareness is still genuinely debated" (the paper does not discuss this)
correctedFact: Two dolphin calves at the National Aquarium in Baltimore were filmed at a mirror over three years. One, Bayley, first showed self-directed behavior at 5.5 months old, earlier than human children usually do (about 12 to 15 months) and much earlier than chimpanzees, which start at around two years or later.

pageTitle: Nocturnal "humming" vocalizations: adding a piece to the puzzle of giraffe vocal communication
quote: We collected over 947 h of audio material in three European zoos ... Hums were rich in harmonic structure, having a deep and sustained sound with an average fundamental frequency of 92.01 ± 25.78 Hz. ... This call type was recorded only during the nocturnal recording sessions. ... Even giraffe keepers and zoo managers stated that they have never heard these vocalizations before.
unsupported: "it sits well inside human hearing" and "They were audible all along" (not stated); "That detail quietly kills a popular claim" (the paper says the infrasound idea lacks systematic evidence but does not say the hums disprove it); "Nobody had listened for 947 hours"
correctedFact: Giraffes were long thought to be nearly silent. Then researchers recorded over 947 hours of audio across three European zoos and found deep, harmonic humming that so far has been recorded only at night, with an average pitch of about 92 Hz. Even the giraffes' own keepers said they had never heard it.
extraPoints: 92 Hz hums are not infrasound, which undercuts the giraffe infrasound claim
note: 92 Hz is above the usual 20 Hz infrasound cutoff, so the arithmetic holds, but the paper never makes the human-hearing point.

pageTitle: Four giraffe species officially recognised in major conservation reclassification – IUCN report
quote: Windhoek, Namibia, 21 August 2025 (IUCN) – A groundbreaking assessment has officially recognised four distinct giraffe species, overturning previous classifications of the world’s tallest land mammal as a single species. ... Historically, giraffe ( Giraffa spp. ) have been classified as a single species with nine subspecies ... Analyses of nuclear and mitochondrial DNA consistently revealed large differences between several giraffe lineages ... Northern giraffe ( Giraffa camelopardalis ) ... Reticulated giraffe ... Masai giraffe ... Southern giraffe
unsupported: "For over a century"; "Genetic work in 2016"; "do not interbreed in the wild"; "separated by differences comparable to those between polar and brown bears" (none on this page)
correctedFact: Giraffes were long classified as a single species with nine subspecies. In August 2025 an IUCN review of genetic, skull and biogeographic evidence formally recognized four: the northern, reticulated, Masai and southern giraffe. DNA studies consistently showed large differences between these lineages, and rivers, rift valleys and dry zones may have kept them apart.
note: The 2016 genetics and the bear comparison trace to Fennessy et al. (2016) in Current Biology, which was not read.

pageTitle: Hemodynamics and Drinking in the Giraffe
quote: integration of flow over time indicated a sequestration in the jugular veins of some 1.2 L of blood in the head‐down position [7]. In our slightly larger animals, this corresponds to about 1.4 L or ≈5% of measured blood volume. ... When heads were lowered for drinking ... (iii) heart rate fell ... It seems most likely, therefore, that esophageal peristalsis drives jugular venous blood towards the heart during drinking at flow rates sufficient to affect cardiac performance.
unsupported: "The textbook explanation, a siphon effect pulling it back, was rejected by a 2025 review because a collapsed vein cannot sustain a siphon" (the 2025 source is an experimental study, not a review, and does not mention a siphon)
correctedFact: When a giraffe lowers its head to drink, about 1.4 liters of blood, roughly 5% of its total supply, pools in the neck veins and its heart rate falls. A 2025 study found a surprising fix: each swallow of water squeezes the valved jugular veins and drives that blood back toward the heart.

pageTitle: Functional cervicothoracic boundary modified by anatomical shifts in the neck of giraffes
quote: The first thoracic vertebra of the giraffe displayed similar shape to the seventh cervical vertebra in general ruminants. The flexion experiment using giraffe carcasses demonstrated that the first thoracic vertebra exhibited a higher dorsoventral mobility than other thoracic vertebrae. ... These anatomical modifications allow the first thoracic vertebra to adopt the kinematic function of a cervical vertebra in giraffes. ... prior studies have criticized the idea of a rib-bearing cervical vertebra in giraffe by the presence of the movable rib in T1: a conclusive criterion for classifying a vertebra as a thoracic vertebra
unsupported: "anatomists have argued for decades" (the paper cites earlier studies on both sides but gives no time span); "The current view" (this is the 2016 study's finding, not a stated consensus)
correctedFact: Giraffes have seven neck vertebrae, the same as you, but the first thoracic vertebra behind them acts like an eighth. It still carries movable ribs, so it counts as thoracic, yet it is shaped like a neck vertebra, bends far more than other chest vertebrae and works as a pivot that extends the neck's reach.

pageTitle: A queen odour mediates reproductive suppression in a eusocial mammal
quote: Naked mole-rats provide a striking example, with reproduction restricted to a single queen, while all other females remain infertile. ... Isopropyl myristate is a low-volatility ester that is enriched in queens and nearly absent from non-breeding animals. ... Daily addition of isopropyl myristate to a queenless colony prevented queen succession, whereas withdrawal triggered aggression and reproductive competition.
unsupported: "dozens of non-breeders who are fertile but suppressed" (the abstract says all other females "remain infertile" and gives no colony size)
correctedFact: Naked mole rat colonies have one breeding queen while every other female stays infertile. A 2026 study found a mechanism: a low-volatility ester called isopropyl myristate, enriched in queens and nearly absent in non-breeders. Add it daily to a queenless colony and no successor rises. Withdraw it and aggression and competition to breed begin.
note: Abstract read on the Max Delbrück Center publication page (Nature 656: 390-398, doi 10.1038/s41586-026-10772-5).

pageTitle: Fructose-driven glycolysis supports anoxia resistance in the naked mole-rat
quote: Under experimental conditions, naked mole-rats tolerate hours of extreme hypoxia and survive 18 minutes of total oxygen deprivation (anoxia) without apparent injury. During anoxia, the naked mole-rat switches to anaerobic metabolism fueled by fructose, which is actively accumulated and metabolized to lactate in the brain. ... Fructose-driven glycolytic respiration in naked mole-rat tissues avoids feedback inhibition of glycolysis via phosphofructokinase, supporting viability.
unsupported: "A mouse in a zero-oxygen chamber dies in under a minute"; "Plants use this pathway"; "No other mammal is known to deploy it as a whole-body rescue" (none in the abstract)
correctedFact: A naked mole rat can survive 18 minutes of total oxygen deprivation without apparent injury. It switches to anaerobic metabolism fueled by fructose instead of glucose, which sidesteps the feedback brake that normally holds back glycolysis, and its brain actively accumulates fructose to burn.
note: Only the abstract was read; the mouse comparison may be in the full paper, which was not opened.

pageTitle: Cultural transmission of vocal dialect in the naked mole-rat
quote: Here we show that the most common naked mole-rat vocalization, the soft chirp, is used to transmit information about group membership, creating distinctive colony dialects. ... Pups fostered in foreign colonies in early postnatal life learn the vocal dialect of their adoptive colonies, which suggests vertical transmission and flexibility of vocal signatures. Dialect integrity is partly controlled by the queen: Dialect cohesiveness decreases with queen loss and remerges only with the ascendance of a new queen.
unsupported: "the whole colony's accent shifts when a new queen takes over" (the abstract says dialect cohesiveness drops when the queen is lost and re-emerges only when a new queen rises)
correctedFact: The naked mole rat's most common call, a soft chirp, carries a colony-specific dialect. The accents are learned: pups fostered into a foreign colony early in life pick up their adoptive colony's dialect. The queen also helps hold it together. When she is lost, the dialect loosens, and it firms up again only when a new queen rises.
extraPoints: Dialect cohesion depends on the queen

pageTitle: Selective Inflammatory Pain Insensitivity in the African Naked Mole-Rat (Heterocephalus glaber)
quote: We show that naked mole-rats, in addition to being insensitive to the effects of capsaicin, are the only known vertebrate without behavioral sensitivity to acid ... In the wild, hundreds of naked mole-rats live in cramped, poorly ventilated chambers, where O 2 levels are low and CO 2 levels are high ... High levels of CO 2 are a noxious stimulus and can stimulate C-fibers by producing tissue acidosis ... No significant differences were observed in the proportion of capsaicin-sensitive neurons between mouse and naked mole-rat.
extraPoints: Naked mole rat nerves detect capsaicin normally, but it never becomes pain behavior
note: "The chilli half of this fact is usually told wrong" is framing, but the paper backs it: capsaicin excites their C-fibers, and pain behavior to capsaicin appears once substance P is supplied.

pageTitle: Individual clown anemonefish shrink to survive heat stress and social conflict
quote: This spanned the world’s fourth global coral bleaching event, which caused temperatures in our study area to exceed the long-term average by 4°C ... Of the 134 clown anemonefish, 71% of rank 1 individuals and 79% of rank 2 individuals shrank at least once ... a single shrinking event increased an individual’s survival probability by 78% compared to individuals that did not shrink, and all clown anemonefish that shrank multiple times survived to the end of the study period
unsupported: "reabsorbing their own tissue" (the paper says it has no information on the mechanism and only suggests tissue resorption as a possibility)
correctedFact: During a marine heatwave that ran 4C above average, researchers measuring 134 wild clownfish found they got shorter, not just thinner. About three quarters of the breeding fish shrank at least once, a single shrinking event raised survival odds by 78%, and every fish that shrank more than once survived.
note: All 134 fish were members of breeding pairs (71% of females and 79% of males shrank), so "dominant fish" reads fine.

publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (2004)
pageTitle: Territory inheritance in clownfish
quote: The clownfish Amphiprion percula forms groups composed of a breeding pair and 0-4 non-breeders. ... Moreover, they form a perfect queue for breeding positions; a queue from which nobody disperses and within which nobody contests. I suggest that queuing might be favoured by selection because it confers a higher probability of attaining breeding status than either dispersing or contesting.
unsupported: "because crossing open reef means being eaten and challenging a bigger fish means losing" (the paper says only that queuing beats dispersing or contesting); "They even limit their own growth to stay unthreatening"; "The wait can last decades"
correctedFact: A clownfish group is a strict size ladder, with a breeding pair on top and up to four non-breeders below. A field study found the non-breeders form a perfect queue for the breeding positions, one nobody leaves and nobody contests, likely because waiting gives each fish a better chance to breed than leaving or fighting.
note: Growth restraint is the subject of Buston (2003, Nature), which was not read. Page read via PMC; abstract cached from PubMed 15252999 (Proc Biol Sci, Biology Letters supplement).

pageTitle: Anemonefish use sialic acid metabolism as Trojan horse to avoid giant sea anemone stinging
quote: Three main hypotheses have been proposed: (i) anemonefish have a thicker mucus layer than other fishes that protect them as a shield; (ii) anemonefish molecularly mimics the composition of anemone mucus; and (iii) anemonefish mucus lacks the trigger for firing sea anemone nematocysts. ... sialic acid levels are specifically decreased in anemonefish mucus but not in other organs ... We conclude that anemonefish regulates the level of sialic acids in their mucus to avoid nematocyst discharge.
unsupported: "extremely low" (the paper says lower, "substantially smaller" than in non-symbiotic damselfish); "They are not wearing a disguise" (the paper lists mucus mimicry as one of three hypotheses and does not rule it out)
correctedFact: Anemone stinging cells are triggered by sugars called sialic acids. A 2025 study found that clownfish keep normal sialic acid levels in their organs but hold them much lower in their skin mucus alone, a lowered signal that may let them slip into the anemone without setting off its stings.
note: A second 2025 study (Scientific Reports, PMC11736139) found sialic acid still present in symbiont mucus and argued the mechanism is more complex than presence or absence, so the finding is contested.

unsupported: Whole fact: the 30-year estimate, the comparison with other damselfish and the decades-long queue
extraPoints: Long female life spans make queuing for a breeding slot worthwhile
note: Searched for Buston and García (2007), Journal of Fish Biology 70: 1710-1719, which search snippets say estimates a 30-year female life expectancy, twice any other reef damselfish. The Buston Lab page lists only the citation and the CORE record returned 403.

pageTitle: Cryoprotectants and Extreme Freeze Tolerance in a Subarctic Population of the Wood Frog
quote: Whereas frogs indigenous to the upper Midwestern United States and southern Canada tolerate freezing only to temperatures as low as -3 to -6°C, frogs from Interior Alaska readily survived experimental freezing to -16°C [6]. We hypothesize that extreme freeze tolerance in this northern phenotype derives in part from an enhanced cryoprotectant system that uses urea, which accumulates in autumn and early winter, before freezing occurs, and glucose ... uremic levels in HYD frogs, which reached 86 μmol ml -1 , were elevated 8-fold.
unsupported: "in the southern part of their range" (the page says the upper Midwestern United States and southern Canada); "The gap comes mostly from urea" (the paper says the tolerance derives in part from a urea and glucose system); "roughly eight times the plasma urea of temperate ones" (the 8-fold rise compares winter-conditioned Alaskan frogs with Alaskan frogs in late summer, not with temperate frogs)
correctedFact: Wood frogs from the upper Midwest and southern Canada survive freezing only to about -3C to -6C. Wood frogs from Interior Alaska readily survive -16C. Part of the gap comes from urea banked before winter: Alaskan frogs raise their plasma urea about eightfold between late summer and winter, before any ice appears.
note: A 2013 Journal of Experimental Biology abstract (PubMed 23966588) puts Alaskan plasma urea at 106 against 28 μmol/ml in Ohio frogs, about four times, so the card's eight-times-temperate figure looks like a misread.

pageTitle: Cryoprotectants and Extreme Freeze Tolerance in a Subarctic Population of the Wood Frog
quote: an enhanced cryoprotectant system that uses urea, which accumulates in autumn and early winter, before freezing occurs, and glucose, which is quickly mobilized from liver glycogen after freezing begins. Both agents colligatively reduce the amount of ice forming in the body ... In Alaskan frogs, glycemia rose to 217 μmol ml -1 during a 48-h bout of experimental freezing to -2.5°C
unsupported: "the instant freezing begins" (the paper says quickly after freezing begins); "at concentrations that would put a mammal in a diabetic coma"; "The ice forms outside the cells, and the sugar keeps what is left inside them dilute enough to survive" (the paper says both agents reduce the amount of ice forming in the body)
correctedFact: Freezing solid takes two chemicals on opposite timetables. Urea builds up through autumn and early winter, before any ice forms. Glucose is the reaction: once freezing begins, the liver quickly breaks down its glycogen and blood sugar soars. Both work by reducing how much of the frog's body turns to ice.

pageTitle: Resumption of physiological functions in the wood frog (Rana sylvatica) after freezing
quote: The first physiological parameter to return was cardiac function, but during the early stages of thawing heart rates were lower than heart rates of unfrozen frogs at comparable body temperatures. Heart rates increased thereafter in conjunction with the rise in frog body temperatures. Spontaneous breathing and hindleg reflexes resumed after cardiac function, but neither response was exhibited by all frogs after the conclusion of the observation periods (3-4 h).
unsupported: "does not warm from the outside in" (not stated); "The heartbeat comes back within an hour and reaches near-normal function within a few hours" (the abstract gives no times for the heart, only that early heart rates were below normal and rose as the frog warmed)
correctedFact: A thawing wood frog does not restart all at once. Its heart is the first thing to come back, beating slowly at first and speeding up as the body warms. Breathing and hind leg reflexes return only after that, and not in every frog even three to four hours later.

publisher: University of Georgia Savannah River Ecology Laboratory
pageTitle: Wood Frog (Rana [Lithobates] sylvatica)
quote: Occurs across most of northern North America, extending into Alaska and above the Arctic Circle—the only amphibian in the Western Hemisphere known to range so far north. It is restricted to the Appalachian Mountains of northern Georgia and northwestern South Carolina. ... Overwinters beneath stumps, logs, or leaf litter.
unsupported: "It gets away with it by freezing rather than digging" (the page does not mention freezing); "not underground and not in water, so it sits through whatever the winter does" (the page says only beneath stumps, logs or leaf litter)
correctedFact: The wood frog lives farther north than any other amphibian in the Western Hemisphere, reaching into Alaska and above the Arctic Circle, yet its range also runs south to the Appalachian Mountains of northern Georgia. It spends the winter tucked beneath stumps, logs or leaf litter.
extraPoints: Overwinters under leaf litter rather than underground or in water
note: Page cached in an earlier batch as e_woodfrog_srel.txt.
